rules.checks: Each sits in an adapters crate.

rules.title: Use cases that save an aggregate must publish its domain events
rules.rationale: A saved aggregate must not keep its events: unpublished, they are lost, and stored on the instance they may later be published out of context. Publishing belongs after the save, in the use case that owns the unit of work - unless the aggregate is proven never to register an event: its whole hierarchy is under scan and no code unit of it, of a helper it calls, or of any other scanned class registering on that aggregate (a nested class it never calls) calls registerEvent; a helper in another top-level class cannot reach the protected method; an unresolved type argument keeps the requirement. Checked per entry path, following calls within the use case class: every entry point that reaches a save - a method callable from outside the class, or one nothing in the class calls - must also reach a publication; a wrapper that publishes does not cover a direct call of the public method it wraps, and a helper two methods share does not connect them. That the publication follows the save and concerns the same aggregate is not established statically. Only DomainEventPublisher.publishAndClearEvents counts as a publication: iterating domainEvents() and calling publish(event), even followed by clearDomainEvents(), separates dispatch from acknowledgement and is not accepted
rules.selects: Functions of types that implement an input port. A port is a field of self, or what an accessor of the transaction unit hands out: unit.things() inside the closure passed to in_transaction or in_transaction_closed, the unit trait found among the bounds of the use case's generics and read through its associated types, generic ones (type Things<'a>) included. The closure returns its future boxed (async move { .. }.scope_boxed()); a call is seen through .await. A local bound by a straight-line let to a port (let things = unit.things();, let repo = &self.things;) counts as that port in its block and the blocks inside, until a later let of the same name shadows it; bindings of if let, while let, match arms, closure parameters and for loops are not followed, and inside their scope they suspend an alias of the same name.
rules.checks: A function that calls save on a repository also hands the aggregate's events on - publish_and_clear_events on a DomainEventPublisher - directly or through a function of the same type. The outbox is the publisher's adapter's: a use case never registers an entry itself.

rules.title: DTOs must not be used in the Domain Layer
rules.rationale: Domain layer should not depend on DTOs (presentation concerns) - Dependency Inversion Principle
rules.selects: Items in every domain crate. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: No item declares or names a type whose name ends with Dto. Paths are read from use declarations - those inside function bodies and blocks too, whose scope is approximated by the whole module - and from every other item, the arguments of vec!, matches!, assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!, debug_assert!, debug_assert_eq!, debug_assert_ne!, format!, write!, writeln!, print!, println!, eprint!, eprintln! and panic! parsed as expressions (and the pattern of matches!). Not seen: paths inside any other macro invocation, and arguments of those macros that do not parse as expressions.

rules.title: DTOs must not be used in the Application Layer
rules.rationale: Application layer should use Command/Query/Response models, not presentation DTOs (Clean Architecture)
rules.selects: Items in every application crate. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: No item declares or names a type whose name ends with Dto. Paths are read from use declarations - those inside function bodies and blocks too, whose scope is approximated by the whole module - and from every other item, the arguments of vec!, matches!, assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!, debug_assert!, debug_assert_eq!, debug_assert_ne!, format!, write!, writeln!, print!, println!, eprint!, eprintln! and panic! parsed as expressions (and the pattern of matches!). Not seen: paths inside any other macro invocation, and arguments of those macros that do not parse as expressions.

rules.title: Use cases that save an aggregate or publish domain events must have a transaction boundary
rules.rationale: The use case owns the unit of work. Saving an aggregate is one business fact, yet the repository may write it as several statements - an aggregate of entities and value objects often spans several tables - and a repository adapter draws no boundary of its own; without one, a failure between the statements leaves half an aggregate behind. Publishing adds a second effect that must fall with the save: integration events are relayed after commit by the framework's after-commit listeners, and their publication is registered in the publishing transaction. Without an active transaction the after-commit listeners are skipped silently and nothing is registered: the use case succeeds, the other contexts never hear of it. The boundary is either declarative transaction metadata (the configured transactional annotation on the class or the executing method) or an explicit TransactionBoundary.inTransaction(...) around load, mutate, save and publish. Checked per entry path, following calls within the class: from every entry point - a method callable from outside the class, or one nothing in the class calls - no route down to the saving, deleting or publishing method may be free of an annotation or a boundary; a covered caller does not cover another route to the same helper, and a boundary on one route does not cover a second route. Whether the save or the publication sits inside the block handed to inTransaction(...) is not visible in ArchUnit's call model, which folds a lambda's body into the enclosing method; that placement stays a review check
rules.selects: Functions of types that implement an input port. A port is a field of self, or what an accessor of the transaction unit hands out: unit.things() inside the closure passed to in_transaction or in_transaction_closed, the unit trait found among the bounds of the use case's generics and read through its associated types, generic ones (type Things<'a>) included. The closure returns its future boxed (async move { .. }.scope_boxed()); a call is seen through .await. A local bound by a straight-line let to a port (let things = unit.things();, let repo = &self.things;) counts as that port in its block and the blocks inside, until a later let of the same name shadows it; bindings of if let, while let, match arms, closure parameters and for loops are not followed, and inside their scope they suspend an alias of the same name.
rules.checks: A function that calls save or delete on a repository, or publish on a DomainEventPublisher, does so inside the closure it passes to in_transaction or in_transaction_closed of a TransactionBoundary (or a function of the same type that does). A port the transaction unit hands out is inside by construction. Rust has no transactional attribute; the explicit boundary is the only form.

rules.reason: Rust has no declarative transaction attribute; the boundary is the explicit TransactionBoundary port, which DCA-USE-012 reads, and the rule selects only declaratively transactional use cases.

rules.title: Use case packages within a module must use one consistent depth (flat or grouped by feature)
rules.rationale: A use case package sits either directly below the application package (application.<usecase>) or one level deeper inside a feature (application.<feature>.<usecase>). A feature is an optional, domain-named group of related use cases - a navigation boundary inside one bounded context, not a layer, module or aggregate owner. Mixing both forms in one module makes it unclear whether a package is a feature, a use case or a leftover; nesting deeper than a feature hides the use case. The rule checks legibility only: it does not infer bounded contexts, feature semantics or aggregate ownership. application.shared holds the context-wide output ports and is not a use case package
rules.selects: Types that implement an input port in every application crate, the shared module excluded. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: All sit at one module depth: application::<use_case> or application::<feature>::<use_case>.

rules.title: Use Case Result Models must not expose aggregate roots or entities
rules.rationale: A result is the use case's answer, not a handle on the model: identity and behaviour stay behind the port; values, enriched models and read models may cross. Checked transitively through nested records, part records anywhere in the application layer (application.shared included), generic type arguments (List<T>, Optional<T>, Map<K,V>) and inherited fields, a generic base class's type parameters resolved as the result binds them
rules.selects: Structs in application crates whose name ends with Result. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: No field type, through generic arguments and into other application structs, implements AggregateRoot or Entity.

rules.title: Use cases must not invoke other use cases
rules.rationale: Ordinary operations do not coordinate other operations; coordination requires explicit transaction and failure semantics
rules.selects: Types that implement an input port.
rules.checks: No field and no parameter of its methods names another input-port trait or a type that implements one, read with the generics of the type, of its impl blocks and of the method (a generic field or parameter stands for its bounds); the building blocks' role traits are not counted.

rules.title: Use cases expose no public operation outside their input port
rules.rationale: The input port describes the complete externally callable operation surface
rules.selects: Types that implement an input port.
rules.checks: No pub method other than the methods of the input-port traits it implements and an inherent associated function that returns Self (the constructor bootstrap calls). A method of another workspace trait - written in the impl or inherited as the trait's default - is reported, as Java reports an unrelated interface's method; impls of std, core, external and building-block traits are not read. The operation lives in the input-port impl.

rules.title: In a module grouped by feature, incoming adapters must drive the commands of one feature only
rules.rationale: Once the application is grouped, the incoming adapter is cut the same way: one controller changes state through the use cases of one feature. A class that drives the commands of two features grows with every use case of both and hides the cut the application already made. Reading a neighbouring feature's query is no reason to cut
rules.selects: Items in the incoming module of every adapters crate, and the input-port traits they name that take a command (the input of a UseCase<..> bound or a method parameter is a type whose name ends with Command) and are declared in a feature: two module levels deep in an application crate, application::<feature>::<use_case>, the shared module excluded. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: The ports one item names belong to at most one feature. An application crate without feature modules selects nothing.

rules.title: Query use cases must not write or publish
rules.rationale: A read never creates. A query has no side effect: it does not create, save or publish, and when nothing exists it answers none. Find-or-create is a command, called where the caller is about to change state; a page or an answer that only shows what exists asks the query
rules.selects: Types that implement an input port whose input is a query. A port is a field of self, or what an accessor of the transaction unit hands out: unit.things() inside the closure passed to in_transaction or in_transaction_closed, the unit trait found among the bounds of the use case's generics and read through its associated types, generic ones (type Things<'a>) included. The closure returns its future boxed (async move { .. }.scope_boxed()); a call is seen through .await. A local bound by a straight-line let to a port (let things = unit.things();, let repo = &self.things;) counts as that port in its block and the blocks inside, until a later let of the same name shadows it; bindings of if let, while let, match arms, closure parameters and for loops are not followed, and inside their scope they suspend an alias of the same name.
rules.checks: No function calls a write (save, delete, remove, add, insert, update, ...) on a repository or store, nor an event publisher.

rules.title: Use cases must not parse raw input into an id
rules.rationale: The adapter turns raw input into the types the input port takes: an id arrives as the id's value type, parsed at the edge or by the value type's own factory, never as text the use case parses. Text that does not parse is a malformed call the adapter answers itself; the use case never sees it
rules.selects: Every application crate.
rules.checks: clippy.toml lists uuid::Uuid::parse_str and uuid::Uuid::from_str under disallowed-methods. Parsing happens in the adapter or in the id's own constructor.

rules.title: Use cases should be stateless (only final fields for dependencies)
rules.rationale: One instance of a use case serves every caller. A field it writes while it runs is shared by the next call and by concurrent ones, and one call's outcome depends on the call before. What a use case holds is set once, by its constructor: the ports and services it is wired with
rules.selects: Types that implement an input port (a trait extending InputPort or UseCase).
rules.checks: No method of their impls takes &mut self, and no field holds interior mutability (Cell, RefCell, Mutex, RwLock, an atomic).

rules.title: Use case results must not be bare primitives or strings
rules.rationale: A use case answers in the application's language: a result type of its own, a value, or a case of a closed result. A bare number, text or flag carries no meaning of its own - an exit code, a status word or a count whose meaning lives in the caller - and it cannot gain a case without changing every caller
rules.selects: impl UseCase<I> blocks, read for their Output type, and the traits that extend UseCase<I, Output = O>.
rules.checks: O, or the success type of a Result it names, is none of String, &str, bool, char or a numeric primitive. () passes - a command with nothing to answer -, and so does a container such as Vec<String>.

rules.title: Diagnostic: use cases and input ports named after a trigger rather than an effect
rules.rationale: A use case is named after its effect, never after its trigger or its caller. When and by whom it runs is the business of the adapter or the consumer that calls it; the same effect reached from a second trigger is the same use case, and a name that carries the trigger invites a second use case for it
rules.selects: Input-port traits and use-case types in application crates, and structs and enums in application crates whose name ends with UseCase, with or without the input-port role.
rules.checks: Informational - lists names that contain a trigger word (On, After, When, Upon, Before followed by a capital) and never fails.

rules.title: Use cases, input ports and published operations must not be named after a field they write
rules.rationale: An operation speaks the domain, not data access. A name after the field it writes (setLimit, updateStatus) says how the data changes, not what the change means; the glossary's verb says that (raise a limit, grant an initial limit), and the caller learns which rules run
rules.selects: Input-port traits and use-case types in application crates, and structs and enums there whose name ends with UseCase, with or without the input-port role; in api crates (the events crate publishes records, not operations, and is not read), the pub free functions, the methods of traits and the pub methods of types (inherent, and of impls of workspace traits declared outside the api crate).
rules.checks: No type name starts with Set or Update followed by a capital, and no function or method name starts with set_ or update_.

rules.title: Domain Packages must not have cyclic dependencies (package-based slice discovery)
rules.rationale: Domain model packages should have clear boundaries and no cycles (Acyclic Dependencies Principle)
rules.selects: One slice per top-level module of every domain crate; the items of the crate root belong to no slice.
rules.checks: The slices form no dependency cycle through the paths their modules name. Between the domain crates of two contexts Cargo refuses a cycle and DCA-STR-004 refuses any edge; inside one crate modules may name each other both ways, so the crate is sliced. Submodules of one top-level module form one slice. Paths are read from use declarations - those inside function bodies and blocks too, whose scope is approximated by the whole module - and from every other item, the arguments of vec!, matches!, assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!, debug_assert!, debug_assert_eq!, debug_assert_ne!, format!, write!, writeln!, print!, println!, eprint!, eprintln! and panic! parsed as expressions (and the pattern of matches!). Not seen: paths inside any other macro invocation, and arguments of those macros that do not parse as expressions.

rules.title: Application Layer must not have cyclic dependencies (package-based slice discovery)
rules.rationale: Application services should have clear boundaries and no cycles
rules.selects: One slice per top-level module of every application crate, the shared module included; the items of the crate root belong to no slice.
rules.checks: The slices form no dependency cycle through the paths their modules name. Cargo refuses a cycle between crates; inside one crate the compiler allows it. A cycle between use cases or features alone is also DCA-CYC-005's; one through the shared module is this rule's only. Paths are read from use declarations - those inside function bodies and blocks too, whose scope is approximated by the whole module - and from every other item, the arguments of vec!, matches!, assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!, debug_assert!, debug_assert_eq!, debug_assert_ne!, format!, write!, writeln!, print!, println!, eprint!, eprintln! and panic! parsed as expressions (and the pattern of matches!). Not seen: paths inside any other macro invocation, and arguments of those macros that do not parse as expressions.

rules.title: Outgoing Adapter Packages must not have cyclic dependencies
rules.rationale: Outgoing adapters should have clear boundaries and no cycles
rules.selects: One slice per module directly below the outgoing module of every adapters crate; items of the outgoing module itself belong to no slice.
rules.checks: The slices form no dependency cycle through the paths their modules name. Cargo refuses a cycle between crates; inside one crate the compiler allows it. Paths are read from use declarations - those inside function bodies and blocks too, whose scope is approximated by the whole module - and from every other item, the arguments of vec!, matches!, assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!, debug_assert!, debug_assert_eq!, debug_assert_ne!, format!, write!, writeln!, print!, println!, eprint!, eprintln! and panic! parsed as expressions (and the pattern of matches!). Not seen: paths inside any other macro invocation, and arguments of those macros that do not parse as expressions.

rules.title: Incoming Adapter Packages must not have cyclic dependencies
rules.rationale: Incoming adapters should have clear boundaries and no cycles
rules.selects: One slice per module directly below the incoming module of every adapters crate; items of the incoming module itself belong to no slice.
rules.checks: The slices form no dependency cycle through the paths their modules name. Cargo refuses a cycle between crates; inside one crate the compiler allows it. A path from the incoming into the outgoing module is DCA-HEX-006's. Paths are read from use declarations - those inside function bodies and blocks too, whose scope is approximated by the whole module - and from every other item, the arguments of vec!, matches!, assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!, debug_assert!, debug_assert_eq!, debug_assert_ne!, format!, write!, writeln!, print!, println!, eprint!, eprintln! and panic! parsed as expressions (and the pattern of matches!). Not seen: paths inside any other macro invocation, and arguments of those macros that do not parse as expressions.

rules.title: Feature and use case packages within a module's application layer must not have cyclic dependencies
rules.rationale: The packages directly below a module's application package are its features (application.<feature>.<usecase>) or, in a flat layout, its use cases (application.<usecase>). A feature is an optional, domain-named group of related use cases; it may depend on another feature in one direction, but a cycle between two of them means the grouping does not carry its weight - the shared concept belongs in application.shared, in the domain, or in one of the two. application.shared is the context-wide port package and is not a slice. The rule does not infer bounded contexts or aggregate ownership from the packages it slices
rules.selects: One slice per operation root of every application crate: the deepest module holding an operation - a struct or enum of the crate with the input-port role or a name ending in UseCase; a module below it joins it. A module that leads to operations without holding one is the feature slice of the first module below the containers. Modules [workspace.metadata.dca] operation-containers lists (a list, empty by default; Java's withOperationContainers) only group operations: they are skipped at the front and left out of the slice's name. The shared module, the crate root and modules outside every operation root belong to no slice.
rules.checks: The slices form no dependency cycle through the paths their modules name: two features, or two use cases of one feature, that name each other, directly or through further slices, are reported. Modules within one crate may depend on each other in both directions; the compiler allows it. An edge between a feature slice and an operation slice nested in it does not count: a Rust module re-exports what its submodules declare (pub use place::PlaceUseCase;) and they use what it declares (use super::Shared;) - Java's feature package holds no such re-export. Paths are read from use declarations - those inside function bodies and blocks too, whose scope is approximated by the whole module - and from every other item, the arguments of vec!, matches!, assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!, debug_assert!, debug_assert_eq!, debug_assert_ne!, format!, write!, writeln!, print!, println!, eprint!, eprintln! and panic! parsed as expressions (and the pattern of matches!). Not seen: paths inside any other macro invocation, and arguments of those macros that do not parse as expressions.

rules.title: Failures declared in the domain layer must implement DomainFailure
rules.rationale: A failure the model raises is a broken business rule and says so through its type; a caller that cannot tell one from the platform's own failures cannot answer either of them properly
rules.selects: Types in every domain crate that implement std::error::Error or carry a derive [workspace.metadata.dca] error-derives lists (written crate::Derive, the crate and the derive's name compared; thiserror::Error by default). Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: Each implements DomainFailure. Rust has no exceptions; a failure is a type returned in Err.

rules.title: Domain and port exceptions reside in the layer whose failure they name
rules.rationale: The base type states which layer owns the failure; declaring it elsewhere puts the vocabulary of that layer outside it and lets an adapter invent failures the application never reports
rules.selects: Types that implement DomainFailure or a port failure (UseCaseFailure, OutputPortFailure, or the classification traits PortFailure and InputPortFailure). Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: A DomainFailure sits in a domain crate, a port failure in an application crate - an output port's failure beside the port, although the adapter that implements the port returns it.

rules.title: Failures declared in the application layer must implement UseCaseFailure or OutputPortFailure
rules.rationale: A use case that cannot serve a request reports why through its type, so that one incoming adapter can map each outcome onto its protocol and another adapter can map the same outcome onto a different one; an output port that declares a failure in its contract names it the same way, so the use case can catch exactly that outcome
rules.selects: Types in every application crate that implement std::error::Error or carry a derive [workspace.metadata.dca] error-derives lists (thiserror::Error by default), and not DomainFailure. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: Each implements UseCaseFailure or OutputPortFailure. Implementing only the classification traits PortFailure or InputPortFailure does not count: a type implements the leaf it is.

rules.title: Domain and port exceptions must not carry prohibited framework metadata
rules.rationale: An exception of an inner layer that carries container, persistence or protocol metadata has decided how the outside answers it, which is the incoming adapter's decision and only its; an annotation that fixes the answer's status decides it for every protocol at once, including the ones the exception knows nothing about
rules.selects: Types that implement DomainFailure, UseCaseFailure or OutputPortFailure, and error types (std::error::Error or a configured error derive) in domain and application crates; the building blocks excluded. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: None carries a derive or an attribute of a crate [workspace.metadata.dca] framework-crates lists, and none implements a trait of one (for example axum's IntoResponse). The orphan rule refuses such an impl in the adapters crate, where both trait and type are foreign, so the source test holds the domain and application crates that depend on the framework. The adapter translates through its own type.

rules.title: Domain and port exception names must stay in the language of their layer
rules.rationale: A failure named after a transport concept is a decision about the answer, taken in a layer that does not know the protocol; the name should say what went wrong, not what the caller should be told
rules.selects: Types that implement DomainFailure or a port failure (UseCaseFailure, OutputPortFailure).
rules.checks: The name contains none of Http, StatusCode, ResponseStatus, Response. The suffix part of the Java rule does not apply: Rust names a failure ...Error by convention.

rules.title: Diagnostic: incoming adapter packages that drive a use case without translating its failures
rules.rationale: A package that drives the application and knows neither failure type nor a case of a closed result either lets everything escape to a generic handler or catches a generic type and answers every outcome the same way; whether it does is not visible in the import model. A use case may return its expected refusals as cases of a closed result instead of throwing them; a switch over those cases is the translation then. An adapter that names the abstract base of the port failures catches them generically and answers every outcome the same way
rules.selects: Modules in the incoming part of every adapters crate that name an input port. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: Informational - lists a module when no item in it names a DomainFailure or UseCaseFailure type nor a variant of a closed result, and never fails. A closed result is an enum an input-port trait answers with - named in an associated-type binding of its bounds (Output = ...) or in a method's return type, through any wrapper such as Result. A variant counts when a path names it through its enum or through a use of it, so a match over the variants is seen; whether the match is exhaustive is left to the compiler. When the workspace has neither a failure type nor a closed result, nothing is listed. It also lists a module that names one of the classification traits PortFailure, InputPortFailure or OutputPortFailure itself - a bound or a trait object over the base is the generic handler that answers every outcome the same way. Paths are read from use declarations - those inside function bodies and blocks too, whose scope is approximated by the whole module - and from every other item, the arguments of vec!, matches!, assert!, assert_eq!, assert_ne!, debug_assert!, debug_assert_eq!, debug_assert_ne!, format!, write!, writeln!, print!, println!, eprint!, eprintln! and panic! parsed as expressions (and the pattern of matches!). Not seen: paths inside any other macro invocation, and arguments of those macros that do not parse as expressions.

rules.title: Diagnostic: failures that carry display data or objects instead of ids and figures
rules.rationale: A failure carries ids and figures, never what a page shows. Its fields are the typed identities and the values the rule compared; a name or a description of the thing an id refers to is resolved by the translation site through the queries it already has. A failure that carries the name decides for every surface what it shows, and one that carries an aggregate or an entity hands the model out through the error path
rules.selects: Types that implement DomainFailure or a port failure, their fields and variant fields.
rules.checks: Informational - lists every field that involves - through its own type or a generic argument, references, slices, arrays, tuples and std's containers and smart pointers (Option, Vec, VecDeque, LinkedList, HashMap, BTreeMap, HashSet, BTreeSet, Box, Rc, Arc, Cow) looked through - a plain string (String, str), a type that implements AggregateRoot or Entity, or any other type that is neither an Id or Value, a number, bool or char, an enum, a time type [workspace.metadata.dca] timestamp-types lists, nor the cause it wraps (a type with a failure role, an error type, a type named Error such as std::io::Error, a trait object or impl bounded by Error such as Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>, the building blocks' PortError), nor a Duration - and never fails. A Vec<u8> passes as Java's list of numbers does; a bare Uuid and any other trait object are listed.

rules.title: Diagnostic: closed use-case results without a case marked as a refusal
rules.rationale: A closed result describes the outcomes a use case can answer with; some of them are refusals, some are not. A result may hold several outcomes of which none refuses - found or nothing found, sent or already sent - and that alone is reason enough to close it. The refusal marker on a case says the request was refused, a meaning the caller answers with or without a transaction, and it is what lets the transaction boundary roll a refusal back like a thrown failure. Whether a case refuses is domain knowledge the type does not show, so a closed result without any marked case is listed for a look, not failed: if one of its outcomes is a refusal and stays unmarked, the transaction commits the writes made before it
rules.selects: Closed results in every application crate: an enum an input-port trait answers with - named in an associated-type binding of its bounds (Output = ...) or in a method's return type, through any wrapper such as Result - as DCA-ERR-006 finds them; an enum that implements std::error::Error, DomainFailure or UseCaseFailure is the failure side and not selected. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: Informational - lists every closed result none of whose variants carries a field whose type implements the building-block trait Refusal, and never fails. A unit variant carries nothing and cannot be the refusing one: a refusing variant wraps a value of a type that implements Refusal, and the result enum implements ClosedResult, whose refusal() match the compiler checks for coverage and for the Refusal bound - that is what TransactionBoundary::in_transaction_closed rolls back on. A listed result is not a finding by itself: one whose outcomes are all successes - found or nothing found - is correct as it is. A struct is no closed result.

rules.title: A domain exception is constructed only in the domain layer
rules.rationale: The model refuses: a domain exception names a business rule the model itself broke off. A use case never invents one. A failure the use case finds - an output port returned nothing, the caller does not own what it names, a precondition on a second aggregate - is the application's, a case of its result or a use-case exception; dressed as a domain failure it claims a rule the model never checked, and the model cannot know what a search found
rules.selects: Every expression in a function body of a module outside the domain crates - application, adapters, api, infrastructure, bootstrap and unplaced crates; #[cfg(test)] items and test targets are not read: a struct literal, a call of a tuple struct or an enum variant, a unit struct or unit variant used as a value, a variant or tuple struct passed as a function, and a call of an associated function without a receiver that returns Self or the type itself, whose type implements DomainFailure. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: None of them names a domain failure - only a domain crate constructs one. Self is not followed: a domain failure declared outside the domain is DCA-ERR-002's finding. A failure the application only passes on (a variant wrapping it, ? or map_err with a conversion) is not a construction. Constructions inside macro invocations, through From/Into conversions or a generic constructor are not seen. An empty selection passes.

rules.title: A port call is never wrapped in a catch of every failure
rules.rationale: A failure has a type, and the code that answers it names that type. A catch of the platform's catch-all or of the port failures' common base around a port call answers every failure alike: a broken rule, an output port's refusal and a defect end in the same branch, and a failure nobody expected is swallowed instead of reaching the one handler that reports it
rules.selects: Every function body - free functions, methods of impl blocks, default methods of traits, closures included - in every application crate and in the incoming module of every adapters crate, and in it every call of a method on a port: a parameter, a local binding whose type is written out, or a field of self, whose type names a trait that carries the input-port or output-port role or a type that implements one, and a field of a parameter whose type is a struct of the workspace holding such a field (ports.add, State(ports): State<Ports> included - a one-field tuple-struct pattern binds its parameter), and what an accessor of a transaction unit hands out inside the closure passed to in_transaction (unit.things()). A field's type is read with the bounds of its struct and of the impl block. A call whose method the receiver's type declares in the workspace - its trait, the traits that trait extends, its own impls - only with an answer other than a Result (a type named ...Result, looked through impl Future, Pin<Box<dyn Future>> and BoxFuture) is no failing call and is not selected (an Option a port answers); a method the workspace does not declare, a building block's included, is selected. A local bound by a straight-line let to a port (let things = unit.things();, let repo = &self.things;) counts as that port in its block and the blocks inside, until a later let of the same name shadows it; bindings of if let, while let, match arms, closure parameters and for loops are not followed, and inside their scope they suspend an alias of the same name. Rust has no try block; a Result is answered where it is consumed. Layers are read from crates with a layer (one crate per layer); in the two-crate form - a context crate without a layer whose layers are top-level modules - this rule reads no layer.
rules.checks: No port call has its failure answered without naming it: not an Err(_) arm, nor a _ or a bare lower-case binding arm the failure reaches (an upper-case identifier is a unit variant or a constant: None), of a match over the call; not if let Ok(..) (which drops the failure) or if let Err(_) over it, nor let Ok(..) = .. else; not let _ = on it; not .ok(), .unwrap_or(..), .unwrap_or_default(), .or(..), .map_or(..), .is_ok() or .is_err() on it, nor .unwrap_or_else, .map_err, .or_else or .map_or_else with a closure that discards its (first) argument (|_| ..); and no port call inside std::panic::catch_unwind, the catch of every panic. The call is seen through parentheses and .await. Propagation with ?, an arm that matches a named failure or takes it in hand (Err(e)), and a map_err whose closure uses the failure pass. A bare binding arm that only cleans up and passes the caught failure on unchanged does not answer it and passes: every exit of its body - the tail and each return, closures and async blocks left out - is the binding itself (other => { undo(); return other; }); one exit that converts, wraps or replaces it (other.map_err(..), .into(), Ok(..)) is reported. A Result bound by a straight-line let to a name (let r = port.run().await;) and answered later - matched, if let, let _ =, or one of the methods above - is checked like the direct form, until a later let shadows the name. Not seen: a Result moved on into another name (let s = r;), a call through a helper of the type's own, and a call on a receiver whose type the suite cannot resolve (an unannotated local initialised otherwise, a return value).

rules.title: The domain holds no shared mutable state
rules.rationale: Rc, Arc, Cell, RefCell, Mutex and RwLock give a value a second owner or a way around &mut. Inside an aggregate they let code outside the root change its parts without the root's invariant check, which is what ownership otherwise prevents.
rules.selects: Every domain crate.
rules.checks: clippy.toml lists std::rc::Rc, std::sync::Arc, std::cell::Cell, std::cell::RefCell, std::sync::Mutex and std::sync::RwLock under disallowed-types; the source test refuses the same types in field types, so a crate without the clippy.toml is held too.

rules.title: Entities compare by identity
rules.rationale: #[derive(PartialEq)] compares every field, which is value equality. Two states of the same entity must be equal and two entities with equal data must not.
rules.selects: Types that implement Entity, aggregate roots included.
rules.checks: The type does not derive PartialEq, Eq or Hash. A manual PartialEq is the expected form; whether it compares only the id is not decidable.

rules.title: Aggregate roots hand out no mutable reference to their parts
rules.rationale: A pub method that returns &mut to an inner entity or collection lets the caller change the aggregate without passing the root's invariant check. Ownership does not prevent it; the signature does.
rules.selects: pub methods of types that implement AggregateRoot.
rules.checks: No return type, through generic arguments, contains a &mut reference.

rules.title: The domain stays synchronous outside its gateways and domain services
rules.rationale: Async is an I/O concern. The domain reaches I/O only through a domain gateway, and only a domain service asks one; everything else in the model stays synchronous, testable and deterministic, and no runtime enters the model.
rules.selects: Functions and methods in every domain crate, except the methods of traits that carry the DomainGateway or the DomainService role and of the impl blocks of types that implement DomainService.
rules.checks: None is async and none returns a type that implements Future. Java and .NET keep the whole domain synchronous; Rust lets a gateway's methods and a domain service's methods be async, with std's Future only. A domain crate without a runtime dependency cannot spawn a task either.

rules.title: The domain reads no clock and no randomness
rules.rationale: A domain that reads the time or draws a random number gives different results for the same input, so its tests depend on the moment they run. The value comes in from the application as a parameter.
rules.selects: Every domain crate.
rules.checks: clippy.toml lists std::time::SystemTime::now, std::time::Instant::now, chrono::Utc::now, chrono::Local::now and rand::random under disallowed-methods, and uuid::Uuid::new_v4 and uuid::Uuid::now_v7.

rules.title: An aggregate's event enum carries one event type per variant
rules.rationale: An event is a type of its own, in every DCA language: it can be named, passed, consumed and checked alone (DCA-ADV-001, DCA-ADV-008 per type). An enum gathers an aggregate's events the way a sealed interface lists its records; a variant with inline fields is an event without a type.
rules.selects: Enums that implement DomainEvent.
rules.checks: Every variant has exactly one unnamed field whose type implements DomainEvent and is not the enum itself.

rules.title: A transaction unit belongs to its use case and hands out only what takes part in the transaction
rules.rationale: A transaction boundary hands its work a unit - the repositories, stores and event publisher that take part in the open transaction. Declared per use case, beside it, the unit says exactly what the use case changes in one transaction; a unit shared between use cases, or one that hands out a clock or a foreign client, hides what the transaction covers and lets the work reach past it. One form - a generic associated type per port, handed out by value - lets a store's adapter hand out a port that borrows the transaction's connection, and keeps two implementations of the same use case alike.
rules.selects: Traits that carry the building-block role TransactionUnit, the building block excluded: the bounds of their associated types, generic ones (type Things<'a>: ... where Self: 'a) included, and the paths in the return types of their methods, Self::<associated type> read through the type's bounds.
rules.checks: Each sits in a use case's module of an application crate - a top-level module other than shared, or below one; extends no trait but TransactionUnit and std's and core's (Send, Sync); declares every associated type with a lifetime parameter (type Things<'a> where Self: 'a) and returns no reference from a method (Self::Things<'_>, not &mut Self::Things); and every trait it binds or returns, std's and core's excepted, carries the role Repository, Store or DomainEventPublisher - a record of the events a listener received is a Store. Whether the unit names exactly what its use case uses is not checked.
